Its three sounds, A-U-M, are held to contain the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, with the silence following it representing a fourth, transcendent state.

The most widely recited mantra of Tibetan Buddhism, invoking Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion; commonly rendered “the jewel is in the lotus,” though its six syllables are understood less as a literal sentence than as a compressed formula, each syllable addressing and purifying one of the six realms of rebirth.

In Mongolian and wider Siberian shamanism, a spirit together with the physical object — often a felt or wooden effigy — made to house it. Ongons are kept, fed, and consulted as some of a shaman's most important helping spirits, frequently understood as the freed souls of ancestors.
The true science of all being. It begins with the study of man, the Microcosm, because man is the highest creation of God and nature with which we become acquainted in the true Ontology.

The consensus, everyday world perceived through the physical senses and governed by ordinary time, space, and cause and effect—the world in which the shamanic journey begins and to which it always returns.

God of the afterlife, the underworld, and resurrection, murdered and dismembered by his brother Seth, then restored by Isis to a partial new life as ruler of the land of the dead. Every deceased Egyptian who passed the judgment of the scales, weighed against the feather of Maat, hoped to be vindicated and “become an Osiris” in the next world.

The Celtic realm of the dead, the fair folk, and the gods, imagined as lying alongside the visible world rather than above or below it — reachable through mist, water, burial mounds, or the liminal turning-points of the year. In Welsh myth it is called Annwn, ruled by a king who keeps justice and lavish hospitality.

A flat board printed with the alphabet, the numbers zero to nine, and the words “yes,” “no,” and “goodbye,” used with a small heart-shaped pointer called a planchette to spell out messages purportedly from spirits of the dead. It grew out of nineteenth-century Spiritualism and the earlier practice of automatic writing, and was patented and sold as a parlor game in 1891. Whatever moves the planchette — a deliberate hoax, unconscious muscular motion, or, as many mystical traditions caution, an unguarded opening to influences the sitter cannot properly discern or control — its real hazard, by Rosicrucian lights, is treating contact with the unseen as a game rather than a discipline requiring the same preparation as any other psychic work.

The serpent or dragon depicted swallowing its own tail, forming an unbroken circle. A Gnostic and alchemical emblem of the unity of all things and the endless cycle of destruction and re-creation through which matter and spirit perpetually change form without ceasing to exist.

A cairn of stones, often crowned with wood and blue prayer scarves, raised at mountain passes and other significant sites across Mongolia and Siberia as the dwelling place of a local spirit. Travelers circle it clockwise and leave an offering or add a stone, in a practice structurally close to the Andean apu and the Sami sieidi.

Mother Earth: the Andean goddess of the earth, fertility, and time, who sustains planting, harvest, and mountain alike and to whom offerings (despacho) of coca leaf, chicha, and food are still poured directly into the ground before any undertaking of consequence. Not a distant creator but an intimate, everyday presence, owed continual small reciprocity rather than occasional grand devotion.

The harmony of man’s accord with the Cosmic which brings a warm glow of contentment throughout one’s whole being. If we have truly gained Peace Profound within our minds, we are able to face all changing conditions with a philosophic and detached attitude.

Man’s capacity to gain impressions, or to cause impressions to register on his consciousness. The objective mind perceives through the sense organs. Psychic perceptions are those perceived by the subconscious other than through the medium of the objective senses. The sum total of our experience colors our perception. When psychic impressions reach us they are interpreted in terms of objective faculties. What is commonly called clairvoyance, for instance, is said to be psychic seeing. Psychic impressions are so interpreted because there is no other way of understanding them. However, dividing them into five divisions like our objective senses is artificial.

The principal search of the alchemists was for a pure and penetrating matter which, when applied to the metals, plants, or vegetables, exalts them. This perfect essence, this soul of matter, imparts its nature to all that is brought into contact with it. This substance which transmits its perfect qualities was called the philosopher’s stone. To the transcendental alchemists, the philosopher’s stone was not a substance but the spiritual gnosis and exalted wisdom whose virtue transmutes man to a higher plane of consciousness and personal power.

Two small glands in the center of the head. Physiologically they have to do with regulating various functions of the body, such as circulation of the blood, growth of the bones and tissues, development of sex and emotional factors. They act essentially as governors. Psychically, they are transformers, stepping down vibrations which come from the psychic plane for objective sensing, and vice versa. By a series of exercises these glands may be perfected in their functioning. Because of its function as a transformer, the pineal gland is called the Third Eye.

Rosicrucians recognize but two planes of existence. One is the worldly, material plane where we live in objective and subjective consciousness. The other is beyond the material, and is that plane where the soul of man functions free from limitations of the body. The latter is sometimes called the Astral, Psychic, or Cosmic Plane; the former the Earthly or Mundane Plane. The Psychic Plane may be reached at any time provided the purpose is pure and noble. It is here we carry on our psychic work as our share in the uplift of mankind.

The negative phase of polarity is the complement of the positive. The negative receives the positive elements and nurtures them to fruition. The result will manifest the blending of the two phases. The negative is passive, static, receptive, and nurturing. The positive is active, creative, dynamic. The coming together of the negative and positive under proper conditions allows for the perfect blending of the two when a third element, the product of the two, is created. Positive applies to an active function or pleroma, that is, fullness of some quality or condition. That which appears by contrast to be of a lesser quality or function is termed negative. Man’s body is a result of the negative side of Cosmic manifestation, just as the soul is the positive manifestation of the Cosmic. The Cosmic is the one central source of divine power. It is dual in its manifestation. The first three fingers of the right hand radiate a positive form of energy, those on the left hand a negative form. Positive vibrations require deep breathing, negative vibrations require exhaling the breath. A positive thought is one which will induce mental or physical action toward the achievement of an end. The opposite is called negative.

The principal surviving sacred narrative of the K'iche' Maya, preserving the creation of the world and of humanity, the trials of the Hero Twins against the lords of the underworld, and the mythic history of the K'iche' people down to the Spanish conquest. Transcribed in the Latin alphabet in the sixteenth century from earlier oral and pictorial tradition, it survived a period in which the Spanish destroyed nearly all other Maya sacred books.

One who is a candidate of a philosophical, religious, mystical, or initiatic school, who pleads for further knowledge or enlightenment and assumes in return certain obligations. One who has advanced through the elementary or Neophyte Degrees of the Rosicrucian teachings is proclaimed a Postulant.

A helping spirit taking animal form, understood to lend its particular strengths, protection, and vitality to the person it accompanies. Retrieving a lost or absent power animal, and restoring it to its keeper, is among the shaman's most fundamental healing tasks.

The formless, chaotic raw material with which the alchemical work begins—unrefined, unworked, containing within it every element and every possibility of what it may become. Symbolically, the prima materia is the self exactly as found: unmanageable, undifferentiated, and not yet subjected to the ordering fire of the Work.

The act of releasing at will, on the psychic plane, the psychic self with its consciousness, mind, powers, and functions, free from the limitations of time and space. Projections are made for the purpose of contacting those whom we wish to aid, or by whom we wish to be assisted and inspired. They are endowed with all the traits, characteristics, and mannerisms that distinguish the personality. A projection will act in full accord with the ethical code characteristic of its soul-personality. Projection is commonly done during sleep, but can be done at will. Sensing and recognizing a projection is also a matter of training. Projection is the phenomenon of being conscious of one’s own being in an immaterial form located in space, near or far, and distinct from his physical entity. It often develops as a kind of dual awareness of self. One is simultaneously aware of his physical being, and then sees an identical image of it standing or seated at a distance. Psychic projection makes possible the extension of man’s powers of perception so that they annihilate time and space. This should not be confused with mental telepathy. It is not the projection or reception of thought, but the projection of the whole psychic self to a distant place. The psychic self then has a direct intimacy with its surroundings.

The psychic counterpart of the physical senses: the faculty of sensitivity by which subtle vibrations, impressions, and psychic phenomena are received and interpreted, apart from the five objective senses. Where ordinary perception depends on the sense organs, psychesthesia is the capacity of the psychic body to register impressions directly, which are then translated into terms the objective mind can use.

The true mystic does not draw a distinction between the material and divine insofar as essence and source are concerned. What lies beyond the range of our physical senses is characterized as the divine and psychic. The psychic realm constitutes octaves or levels of the same stream of consciousness as those to which our receptor senses respond, but which are of a higher frequency than those of the physical senses.

The term is really a misnomer but it helps to convey the idea. The psychic body is an aggregate of the higher, more sensitive levels of consciousness that permeate man’s being. It is that consciousness and intelligence which accounts for the involuntary actions of the body. The psychic body is a kind of conscious field that corresponds to the physical body. The silver cord is the connecting link between the physical and psychic organisms so that the two may work cooperatively. The sympathetic nervous system is the medium for the subconscious mind to carry out the commands in the psychic body. The psychic body carries with it a behavior pattern from the most primitive states of mankind, and the pattern of Cosmic order of which this energy of life consists. There are seven important psychic centers or glands which receive and transform the psychic vibrations which we receive into grosser ones, causing us to have a consciousness of them. These are the thyroid, the pituitary, the pineal, the adrenals or suprarenals, the thymus, the parathyroids, and the pancreas.

A phenomenon related to the higher levels of consciousness, beyond or behind those levels that respond to the physical world only. It may originate as a transmission from other minds or from attunement with Cosmic forces and intelligences outside the individual organic being, or from a realization of the Cosmic consciousness. To realize a psychic experience, the phenomenon has to be translated into terms of our sense faculties and associated ideas.

From the Rosicrucian point of view, psychology is the science which treats of the soul, its attributes—mind and consciousness—and its purpose, place, and function, as well as its influence in our lives as regards habits, their formation, adoption, rejection, or transmutation; together with the action and interaction of the two phases of mind and other forms of psychic and mental existence.
A guide of souls: the shamanic role of journeying to locate the spirit of someone recently deceased, or one who has lost their way after death, and escorting it safely to the realm of the ancestors.

The “weighing of the soul”—the ancient Egyptian rite, depicted in the Book of the Dead, in which the heart of the deceased was weighed on a scale against the feather of Maat in the presence of Osiris. A heart heavier than the feather, burdened by wrongdoing, condemned its owner; a heart in balance with truth passed into eternal life. The scene is the archetype for every later doctrine of self-examination and moral accounting.

The vital energy or life-breath held in Chinese thought to animate all things, flowing through the body along channels called meridians and through the wider world as the animating force behind growth, change, and health. Its free, balanced flow is the aim of practices from acupuncture to tai chi to qigong.

The feathered-serpent god of wind, learning, the priesthood, and the planet Venus, credited in some accounts with creating humanity from the bones of a previous age moistened with his own blood. Closely related to Kukulkan of the Maya, and, following the Spanish conquest, entangled in colonial-era legend with prophecies of a returning god.

The “fifth essence,” beyond the four material elements of earth, air, fire, and water—the pure, incorruptible substance the alchemists believed underlay and animated the other four. Quintessence stands for whatever remains of a thing, or of a person, once everything inessential has been drawn off.

A recording device of knotted, colored cords used across the Andes, especially by the Inca, to keep census figures, tribute accounts, calendars, and, many scholars now believe, narrative and historical information encoded in knot type, position, and color rather than in written script. Because no comprehensive key to its encoding survives, much of what a given quipu recorded remains undeciphered — a system of memory built not on symbols read left to right, but on relationships tied directly into physical form.

The foretold end of the Norse cosmos: a final battle in which most of the gods, giants, and monsters of the mythology destroy one another, the world burns and sinks beneath the sea — and, in the fuller telling, rises again afterward, green and renewed, with a handful of gods and two human survivors to begin the world anew.

The primal sky father and earth mother of Maori cosmology, locked in so tight and continuous an embrace at the world's beginning that their children, the gods, grew up crowded in permanent darkness between them. It was Tane who finally forced them apart, pushing his father high into the sky and pressing his mother down into the earth, letting light and space into the world for the first time — the primordial separation from which everything else follows.

The Polynesian name for Easter Island, the remote South Pacific island whose Rapa Nui people carved and raised the moai — the monumental stone ancestor figures set on platforms called ahu to face inland over their descendants and channel mana for the community's protection and prosperity.

Deductive or structural reasoning is the function of the knowing mind; inductive or genetic reasoning is of the cognition. Induction is progressing from results to cause. Its weakness is in the process. Deduction consists of logical steps forward from the primary idea to its ultimate conclusion. Its weakness is in the premise. The objective reasons by all processes, the subconscious mind tends to reason deductively.

The two-natured figure—half king, half queen—that emerges from the Conjunction, uniting Sulphur and Mercury, sun and moon, masculine and feminine, into a single completed being. Its Latin name means the “double thing”: not a compromise between opposites but their full, simultaneous embodiment in one form.

The Rosicrucian doctrine of reincarnation is that the soul-personality is reborn in human form again after a particular period on the Cosmic plane. At transition this soul-personality moves into the Cosmic plane along with the Universal Soul Essence. There it remains until the right time for another incarnation of the Soul in another physical body. The personality remains conscious of itself on the Cosmic plane and can carry on the psychic manifestations of itself more easily than on the earth plane. Each personality may incarnate many times, the limit being unknown. Reincarnation should not be confused with transmigration. The personality never retrogrades or enters the bodies of lower animals. The mystical doctrine underlying the necessity of reincarnation is the absorption of the soul-personality into the Universal Mind, the process of perfecting the soul-personality. Life by life through varied experiences the personality unfolds as we become more and more conscious of the Cosmic intelligence within us. When our soul-personality is equivalent to the soul force within us, then perfection is realized. We are then one with the consciousness of the Cosmic. At such a time, rebirth is no longer necessary.

An honorific meaning “precious one,” given to a highly respected Tibetan Buddhist teacher — most often a recognized tulku, though also, at times, an accomplished teacher recognized for realization rather than lineage.

A ceremony marking a person's movement from one social or spiritual state to another, classically structured in three phases: separation from the old status, a liminal period of testing or ordeal, and reincorporation into the community in the new one.

Ritualistic ceremonies are a combination of acts and symbols designed to induce a psychic and emotional experience. They are not an intellectual presentation of ideas intended to convey knowledge. Every mystical ritual is a well-organized psychological plot designed and tested to produce particular psychic and emotional experiences upon the part of the individual. Rituals are prescribed patterns of action to discipline and impress the mind with certain experiences to which importance has been attached.

God of cultivated food plants, especially the kumara (sweet potato), and of peace — invoked to end conflict as readily as to bless the harvest, since a settled peace and a planted crop depend on each other.

An abstract or artificial symbol consisting of two elements. It symbolizes the physical body of man with arms outstretched, facing the light. In the center, where the horizontal arm joins the verticle staff of the cross, is superimposed the rose. It represents the soul-personality. The partially unfolded rose alludes to the evolving consciousness as it receives the Greater Light.

The fourth and final stage of the Magnum Opus, in which the work is completed and the philosopher's stone is achieved—traditionally pictured, like gold itself, in the color red. Rubedo represents full integration: the base and the noble, the material and the spiritual, fused into a single, completed whole.

The angular letters of the earliest Germanic writing systems, each carrying not only a sound but a name and a layer of symbolic meaning, used for inscription, memorial, and, in magical use, divination and charm-making — casting or drawing runes to read intention or fate into their fall.

The study and use of geometric forms and proportions — the circle, the vesica piscis, the golden ratio, the Platonic solids, the Flower of Life — held across many cultures to encode the same underlying order found in living structures, celestial motion, and the fabric of matter itself. Found alike in Egyptian temple plans, Gothic cathedrals, Islamic tiling, and Hindu yantras, sacred geometry treats form and proportion as a kind of visible mathematics of the Cosmic, in which how a thing is shaped is inseparable from what it means.

Sacred geometric and figural tattoos, applied by a monk or lay master (an ajarn) chanting the accompanying mantra as the design is hand-tapped into the skin with a long needle. Originating with Khmer warriors who believed the designs granted protection in battle, sak yant spread through Cambodia, Thailand, and Laos and remains widely practiced today, notably around Chiang Mai, as a living fusion of Buddhist, Hindu, and animist symbolism.

The festival marking the boundary between the light and dark halves of the year, when the veil between the world of the living and the Otherworld was held to be at its thinnest, making it a time for honoring the ancestors. Its customs passed largely intact into modern Halloween.

The beginningless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth, driven by karma and ignorance, in which beings across Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology are held to wander until liberation is attained. Buddhism describes samsara as inherently marked by suffering (dukkha), impermanence, and the absence of any fixed, permanent self passing through it.

In each Lodge it is the place or condition located between the Shekinah and the Altar. It is kept holy and reserved exclusively for certain parts of sacred ceremonies or convocations and must not be used for other purposes. Trespassing in the Sanctum is forbidden to all but the Master or Colombe and is a “serious and grievous error bringing a lesson from the Cosmic upon the Lodge and the trespasser.”

A sanctuary within the home, a temple dedicated to the highest ideals and concepts of which one is capable. It is a refuge, a place to which you may retire from the usual conditions with which you are confronted, free from encumbrances and distractions. It is as well a little eminence upon which you can stand to look up to the Cosmic. A sanctum is a place you have consecrated to your better self, to your God, to your ideals. Entering it constitutes a rite of transition from the world of your usual thought to one of devotion, where you may receive and learn.

The operation of dividing a substance into its constituent parts—the subtle from the gross, the useful from the useless—so that each may be purified and later rejoined in truer proportion. Separation is the discernment that must precede any honest reconjunction.

The seven metals known to the ancient world—gold, silver, mercury, copper, iron, tin, and lead—each paired with one of the seven classical planets (Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and held to share its nature and influence. The alchemist's transmutation of “base” lead into “noble” gold is worked, symbolically, on this same sevenfold ladder within the self.

The active, feminine, creative power of the divine, without which the gods are said to be inert — worshipped both as an abstract cosmic force and as the great goddess in her many forms, from gentle nurturer to fierce destroyer.

A man or woman who, through calling, ordeal, or training, has learned to move at will between ordinary and non-ordinary reality, acting as healer, diviner, and psychopomp for their community. The word derives from the Tungusic saman, “one who knows,” or, in some readings, “one who is set in motion.”

The deliberate practice of entering a light trance, usually induced by monotonous drumming or rattling, in order to travel in non-ordinary reality—descending to the Lower World or rising to the Upper World—to seek guidance, healing, or a lost part of oneself, and to return with it intact.

The initiatory crisis—often a severe illness, breakdown, or series of losses—through which many shamans in many cultures are said to receive their calling. The healer's authority is understood to come precisely from having been broken and having survived, not in spite of the wound but because of it.

The particular altered state, distinct from both ordinary waking awareness and sleep, in which the shamanic journey takes place: the practitioner remains aware and later remembers the experience fully, while perceiving and interacting with non-ordinary reality as directly as the physical senses perceive the physical world.

The oldest known family of spiritual practice, found in cultures worldwide, in which a practitioner enters a deliberately altered state of consciousness to journey between worlds, contact helping spirits, and bring back healing, guidance, or lost parts of the soul on behalf of an individual or the community.

In the center of the Lodge, where lines from the four points of the horizon would meet, is the heart of the soul of the Temple. This is the fifth point, occupied by the Sacred Triangle, the Shekinah. The Shekinah is the symbolical place representing “the Presence of God in our Midst.” It is “the point within the inner circle,” the outer circle being the Temple, the inner circle the Lodge. Thus, it is the triangle within two circles. The Shekinah represents the presence of the concentrated power of the Holy Assembly of the Cosmic in the center of the Temple.

One of Hinduism's principal deities, the destroyer within the great triad alongside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver — though destruction, in this reading, clears the ground for renewal. Shiva is equally the supreme ascetic and yogi, lord of meditation, dance, and the dissolution that precedes rebirth.

The historical founder of Buddhism, born a prince in the fifth or sixth century B.C. in what is now Nepal, who renounced his household life after encountering old age, sickness, and death, and after years of ascetic practice attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, becoming the Buddha, “the awakened one.” His subsequent teaching, the dharma, is the foundation from which Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana Buddhism all descend.

A natural feature — most often an unusually shaped rock, cliff, or tree — venerated across Sami territory as the seat of a local spirit, and given offerings of reindeer blood, antlers, or other gifts in exchange for good fortune in hunting and fishing.

This represents the Obligation and Oath taken by all initiates at the time of the First Degree Initiation, and at other times in ceremonies and convocations. Instructions for making the sign may be found in the Neophyte Guide and the Rosicrucian Manual.

The brightest star in the night sky, worshipped by the Egyptians as the goddess Sopdet (Sothis to the Greeks) and closely identified with Isis. Its heliacal rising, appearing just before dawn after months of invisibility, coincided with the annual flooding of the Nile and marked the start of the Egyptian year; because the Egyptian calendar and Sirius's rising drifted out of step and realigned only once every 1,460 years, this longer span became known as the Sothic cycle.

It is located in the center of the abdomen and is part of the sympathetic nervous system. It is not one of the seven important psychic centers, but is important in its physical and psychic functioning. It requires many years of careful development of this plexus to make it of real value in true mystical work.

The Divine essence or Cosmic intelligence which permeates man. There is but one Soul in the universe, the soul of God, the Living, Vital Consciousness of God. Within each living being there is an unseparated segment of that universal Soul. This is the soul of man. It never ceases to be a part of the universal Soul. The soul is the divine consciousness which accompanies the vital life force. It is an extension of God in man. Man can respond to it, but he cannot control or possess it. Every human is bound by this universal soul force to every other mortal.

A healing journey undertaken on the understanding that trauma can cause a part of a person's vital essence to split off and remain lost in non-ordinary reality. The shaman journeys to find that missing part and bring it home, restoring what the person could not recover alone.

The personality is Self, and Self is an expression of the soul within the body of man. It is the manifestation of one’s response to the unseparated segment of the universal soul with which man is imbued. The personality is the image and the soul the object. The personality as an image is but a reflection of the soul. It is not a perfect image because it needs to reflect itself through the encompassing elements of the human organism and objective consciousness.

Like time, space depends upon the relation of our consciousness to other things. Space appears as an area between the objects which we perceive and ourselves; it falsely conveys the notion of having a definite reality. Unconsciously man has associated the duration of time with the extent of space. Because man measures time and space by means of his five senses, which are undependable, he is a victim of delusion or deception.

A universal essence (energy) pervading all matter and manifesting in many ways, such as cohesion, adhesion, etc. It is a divine, universal essence like soul, but of a lower rate. Spirit is the negative polarity of Nous, but is likewise dual and has a positive aspect. When the vital life force combines with the manifestations of spirit, we have life. Spirit is a vibratory energy, the number of vibrations determining the nature of a thing.

The operation in which a solid is heated directly to vapor without passing through a liquid state, then allowed to solidify again in purer form higher in the vessel. Sublimation pictures the rising of the coarse into the refined—matter lifted, without loss, onto a higher plane.

A subtle command, a request, a wish, an order, or a law of one’s objective mind to the subconscious. Mental suggestion means that through the power of will a certain desire is directed or concentrated upon a given point. When the objective consciousness is at rest, the subconscious is susceptible to suggestion. Autosuggestion is suggestion to oneself.

Lord of the Andean underworld and of the dead, ruling a realm called Ukhu Pacha. Not evil in the Christian sense before colonial reinterpretation recast him as a devil-figure, but a powerful, ambivalent force who, propitiated correctly, was believed to protect miners and travelers passing through his domain.

A device or object used to represent an idea. It is the embodiment of a thought which it concisely suggests. Natural symbols are those things in nature which by experience have come to represent a phenomenon. Artificial symbols are those which men devise to depict some idea.

A neurological phenomenon in which stimulation of one sense involuntarily triggers an experience in another — hearing a color, tasting a shape, seeing a specific hue for a given number or day of the week. Occurring spontaneously in a measurable minority of people, synesthesia interests mystical traditions as a naturally occurring instance of the senses crossing and blending, offered by some as a physiological hint at the kind of unified, cross-modal perception that psychesthesia and other psychic faculties are said to reach through disciplined practice rather than involuntary wiring.

God of the forests, birds, and all living things that grow from the earth, and the separator of his parents Rangi and Papa. Having pushed the sky away from the earth to make room for light, Tane clothed his mother Papa in trees and set the birds among them — the god most directly responsible for the visible, growing world as it now stands.

God of the sea, lakes, rivers, and every creature that lives in them, one of the great atua born of Rangi and Papa. As guardian of the largest single domain in the Maori cosmos, Tangaroa's favor governs fishing, voyaging, and safe passage across water in a culture whose history and settlement were carried by sea.

The central concept of Taoism: the ineffable, underlying principle or path by which the universe unfolds, prior to and beneath every particular thing, force, or event. The opening line of the Tao Te Ching warns that any tao which can be fully named or spoken is not the eternal Tao — it is to be lived and aligned with, not defined.

Sacredness, restriction, or a state charged with spiritual consequence — a person, place, or object under tapu must be approached according to strict protocol, since to violate it is understood to bring real, often physical, harm. Tapu functions as an ethical and ecological regulator as much as a religious one, restricting behavior that would otherwise cause harm to people or resources.

God of wind, storm, and weather, the one child of Rangi and Papa who opposed his siblings' decision to separate their parents. In grief and fury he pursued his brothers across sea, forest, and field with storms — explaining, in the myth, why wind still troubles Tangaroa's sea and Tane's forest.

Often translated “virtue” or “power,” te is the Tao's efficacy as it is realized and expressed in a particular person or thing — not moral virtue in the Western sense of obedience to a rule, but the natural integrity and quiet potency of something, or someone, fully and authentically itself.

“Smoking Mirror”: a god of night, sorcery, discord, and fate, whose obsidian mirror was said to reveal hidden truths, including a person's own hidden nature, to whoever looked into it. Capricious rather than simply malevolent, he granted kingship and fortune as readily as he withdrew them.

A world-destroying flood, recounted with striking consistency across cultures that had no contact with one another: the Sumerian Ziusudra, the Babylonian Utnapishtim, the Hebrew Noah, the Greek Deucalion, and the Hindu Manu each survive a divinely sent flood by building a vessel and preserving a remnant of life to begin again. Whether read as shared memory of real post-glacial flooding, independently invented moral parable, or both, the deluge is one of the most widespread single story patterns in world mythology.

A goddess of fate, sovereignty, and war, who appears both singly and as a trio of related goddesses. Closely tied to Samhain and the thinning of the boundary between the worlds, she embodies the destructive, transformative aspect of life that clears the ground for what comes next.

The three sisters — Urd (what has become), Verdandi (what is becoming), and Skuld (what shall be) — who dwell beneath Yggdrasil and spin, weave, or carve the fate of every being, gods included; a Norse counterpart to the Greek Fates, and a picture of destiny as something continuously made, not fixed in advance.

“The teaching of the elders”: the oldest surviving Buddhist school, dominant today in Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia, which holds closest to the earliest recorded discourses of the Buddha and emphasizes individual liberation through monastic discipline, meditation, and direct insight into the nature of suffering.

The ibis-headed Egyptian god of wisdom, writing, magic, and the moon, credited by tradition with inventing language and recording the words and deeds of the gods as divine scribe. Around the third century B.C. the Greeks identified Thoth with their own Hermes; the fused figure, Hermes Trismegistus, became the reputed author of the Hermetic writings and the founding teacher of the Western esoteric tradition.

The duration of consciousness, or the period that consciousness requires to be aware of the material things of life. Time is not a material element of the universe; it does not have an external reality. The objective consciousness and the inner or subconsciousness of man have a different sense of “duration.” Time and space are illusions of the objective mind—but not illusions to be denied, for they are essential.

God of rain, water, lightning, and agricultural fertility, propitiated with particular urgency in a landscape where the failure of the rains meant famine; also feared as the sender of floods, drought, and the lightning bolt alike.

God of the sun in its present age, believed to require ongoing offerings of blood and hearts to keep him strong enough to continue his daily journey across the sky and hold off the darkness that had already ended four previous worlds.

A meditation practice of “sending and taking”: the practitioner breathes in, deliberately, the suffering of another being, and breathes out relief, compassion, or well-being toward them, reversing the ordinary instinct to draw comfort inward and push pain away.
An animal, plant, or natural object held to stand in a special kinship relationship with a person, family, or clan, sharing its qualities with them and receiving reverence and protection in return.

The quality of being beyond, above, or independent of the material universe and ordinary human experience. Applied to the Divine, transcendence holds that God or the Cosmic exceeds and is not exhausted by creation—exalted beyond full human grasp. In mystical use, a transcendent experience is one that carries consciousness beyond its ordinary, earth-plane limitations.

Since there is no death in natural or spiritual law, the term is erroneous and contradictory. The great change that takes place is a transition and transposition of the component parts which constitute the living human being. This transition consists of separation of the dual parts of man, soul and body.

Both an alchemical and a mystical term. It may be mental, physical, and spiritual. It means the changing of the vibratory nature of a material element, or the vibratory expression of a spiritual manifestation so that the manifestation is different after the change. The highest demonstration of transmutation is the changing of the baser elements of our physical natures into the highest ideal expressions and of our desires and thoughts into living spiritual ideals.

The three essential principles from which Paracelsus taught all matter, physical and spiritual, is composed. Sulphur is the principle of combustibility, soul, and active will; Mercury the principle of fluidity, spirit, and transformation; Salt the principle of fixity, body, and permanence. Neither element in the chemical sense nor mere substance, the three are read as the triune nature of every created thing—body, soul, and spirit in one.

A symbol of the numeral 3, and of perfection in the use of natural laws or in any undertaking. There are two phases or qualities of things. From their blending comes a third or new condition or state, having the attributes of both of the separate ones.

Whatever is real to us is truth. Whatever lacks reality is not accepted as truth. Nothing is true merely because it has the sanction of tradition. The intimacy of an experience must include one of two factors: First, the full extent of our powers of perception; second, the full capacity of our reasoning.

A recognized reincarnation of a deceased, realized Buddhist teacher, identified in childhood — often through tests involving the previous teacher's possessions — and raised to continue that teacher's line of instruction. The Dalai Lama is the best known example of a tulku lineage to those outside Tibetan Buddhism.

In Tibetan Buddhist and later Theosophical usage, a thought-form or being deliberately created through sustained, disciplined visualization, vivid enough to take on an appearance of independent existence to its creator and, in some accounts, to others as well.

The Tungusic-speaking peoples of Siberia (today chiefly the Evenki) whose word saman — “one who knows” — was carried into Russian and then into European languages as the general term “shaman.” Their own practice, involving trance, drumming, and journeying to a cosmos divided into upper, middle, and lower worlds, is one of the sources anthropologists later drew on in describing shamanism as a cross-cultural category.

One of the three shamanic worlds, reached by journeying upward beyond the sky, where sages, teachers, and celestial guides are traditionally encountered—an ethereal realm of expanded vision and long perspective.

An alchemical motto formed from the initial letters of the Latin Visita Interiora Terrae, Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem: “Visit the interior of the earth, and by rectifying, you will find the hidden stone.” Read spiritually, it is an instruction to descend into one's own depths—not to escape them—as the only route to the stone one is seeking.

“The diamond vehicle”: the tantric branch of Buddhism, dominant in Tibet and the Himalayan region, which builds on Mahayana teaching with esoteric ritual, visualization, mantra, and initiation by a qualified teacher, aiming at a more direct and accelerated path to the same enlightenment Mahayana pursues over many lifetimes.
related: Bardo Thodol (Tibetan Book of the Dead)

entries.explanation: The great hall of the slain, presided over by Odin, to which warriors who die bravely in battle are carried by the Valkyries to feast, fight, and heal each day in preparation for standing at Odin's side at Ragnarok.

A periodic impulsation or wavelike oscillation of forces. Vibrations occur in solids, liquids, air, and in electromagnetic phenomena. According to Rosicrucian ontology, all being is vibratory. There are two forms of vibrations; those which emanate from the universal force or energy of the universe, and those which are set in motion by mental or psychic impulses. Everything which exists in this world is sensed by us or known to us through vibrations which reach our consciousness.

The phenomenon of detecting the physical and mental qualities of a person from inanimate objects once in their possession. Objects acquire the magnetic influence of the human aura of those in whose possession they have been. These vibrations affect our sympathetic nervous system. We become conscious of certain psychic impressions of the personalities whose auras were in contact with the material substance.

The supreme creator god in Inca and pre-Inca mythology across the Andes region of South America, held to have shaped the earth, the sky, and the first beings out of formless dark, then to have wandered the world teaching before departing across the western sea, promising an eventual return. Often described as a bearded, light-skinned wanderer-god, a detail later Spanish chroniclers seized upon and read, controversially, into their own arrival.

The preserver within the triad, who sustains cosmic order across the ages and is held to descend to earth in avatars — Rama and Krishna foremost among them — whenever that order falls into serious decline.

A solitary rite of passage, typically involving fasting, prayer, and isolation in a natural setting for several days, undertaken to seek guidance, purpose, or a helping spirit directly, without an intermediary. Practiced with variations across many Native nations, most often to mark the passage into adulthood or to seek direction at a turning point in life.

Consists, mystically, of painting on the screen of consciousness an image, simple or complex. A person paints on the screen of his mind representations of that which he desires. In his mind’s eye he gradually sees a picture of his desire. When he sees the picture as complete as he can visualize it, he dismisses it entirely from his mind. This transfers the image from the objective to the subconscious and thence outward into the Cosmic. The individual, by the positive thought transmitted to the Cosmic will be drawn to those conditions and circumstances by which he will bring the visualization into reality in objective ways. The image on the screen must become so realistic as to be actualized.

The form of energy which vitalizes the human body at the moment of birth and which leaves at the moment of transition. It is not spirit energy which exists in all matter, and which does remain in the human body after transition. The positive polarity of Nous manifests as vital life force. It is this which animates matter, brings into existence the living energy. An attribute of the vital life force is consciousness. It is infinite and unlimited and becomes soul when in man.

The oldest form of ceremonial formula known to man employed sounds and syllables to bring about attunement. Spoken properly, these syllables produce unusual results. They start certain rates of vibrations in the room which harmonize with other vibrations of the universe and affect a certain condition connected with the aura. Vowel sounds produce vibrations that pass through one’s own being to stimulate the psychic centers and to produce the beneficial effects explained in our teachings.

The spirit or soul: the non-physical dimension of a person that connects them to their ancestors, their descendants, and the wider spiritual world, and that survives the death of the body. Wairua is often described as flowing between two waters, the pure and the troubled, reflecting a person's spiritual state at a given time.

The Lakota name for the great holy mystery underlying and pervading all things — not one god among many but the encompassing sacred itself, of which the sun, the earth, the four directions, and every lesser spirit are understood as aspects or expressions.

Genealogy — but understood far more broadly than a family tree: the layered lines of descent and relationship linking every person, tribe, natural feature, and even abstract concept back through the gods to Rangi and Papa themselves. To recite one's whakapapa is to state exactly where, and to whom, one belongs in a single connected order of things.

The cycle of eight festivals by which modern Druidic and pagan traditions mark the turning seasons: four fire festivals (Samhain, Imbolc, Beltane, Lughnasadh) and four solar festivals (the solstices and equinoxes), together forming a complete round of death, dormancy, growth, and harvest.

The work of the Order consists of studying, testing, and teaching such laws of God and Nature as will make our members Masters in the Holy Temple (the physical body), and Workers in the Divine Laboratory (nature’s domains). This enables us to render more efficient help to those who do not know, and who need or require help and assistance. Each initiate has an obligation to serve, making it imperative to study and practice the laws taught in our Order, and to apply them at every opportune time.

A process by which the soul of man becomes consciously aware of its oneness with that of God. It gives him a realization of his part in the great scheme of all that is. Worship, never an end in itself, should be the evidence of man’s desire to bring himself to a higher plane of realization of the ideal worshipped. Worship is essentially a process or condition which exists within man. While certain physical aids are valuable in creating a favorable environment, real worship must be carried on within the sanctum of man’s own being.

“Non-action,” or effortless action: acting in such complete accordance with the natural flow of the Tao that the action requires no forcing, no excess effort, and no fighting against the grain of things. Wu wei is not passivity but exactly timed, minimal, unresisted right action.

The Maya underworld, “place of fright,” ruled by twelve lords under Ah Puch and reached by a harrowing road of trials — rivers of blood and scorpions, houses of jaguars, bats, and knives — that the Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh must out-think and survive in order to defeat death itself.

The immense ash tree at the center of the Norse cosmos, its roots and branches connecting all nine worlds — among them Asgard, home of the gods, and Midgard, the world of humans — and beneath whose roots the Norns tend the well of fate.

The two complementary, interdependent forces whose interplay Taoism holds to generate all phenomena: yin dark, receptive, and yielding; yang bright, active, and assertive. Neither exists without the other, each contains the seed of its opposite, and their endless interchange, not the triumph of one over the other, is the natural order itself.

An abrupt return to near-glacial cold, lasting roughly from 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, that interrupted the general warming at the end of the last Ice Age. Its cause remains debated: mainstream climatology points to a sudden influx of glacial meltwater disrupting ocean currents, while a minority, more speculative hypothesis proposes a fragmenting comet impact and popularly connects the period's floods and climate chaos to the flood myths preserved across many world cultures, and to Plato's account of the sinking of Atlantis. Most archaeologists and geologists regard the comet-impact version as unproven.
